parts.title: Booking a Canal Narrowboat Holiday
parts.scenario: A man phones a holiday company to book a week on a canal narrowboat for his family.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lorna
voices.desc: Booking adviser at a canal holiday company — female, 40s, warm, efficient, candid; British accent (southern English)

voices.label: Martin
voices.desc: Caller — male, late 30s, friendly, a little unsure, good-humoured; British accent (Midlands)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a holiday company to book a canal narrowboat holiday. First, you have some time to look at Questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [telephone rings twice, then the line clicks open] [bright, professional] Good morning, Hartwell Waterways, Lorna speaking. How can I help?

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [friendly, slightly unsure] Oh, hello. I'm hoping to book a narrowboat for a week this summer. I've never done anything like this before, so, er, bear with me.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [warm, reassuring] Not at all, most of our customers are first-timers. Let me just take a few details first. Could I have your name?

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: Yes, it's Martin Wardrop.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [careful, checking] Is that spelt like the furniture? W-A-R-D-R-O-B-E?

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [light laugh] Everybody says that. No, it's W... A... R... D... R... O... P. There's no E on the end.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [repeating slowly, as if typing] W... A... R... D... R... O... P. Lovely. And how many of you will be on the boat?

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [sighs] Well, it was going to be six. My sister and her husband were coming, but they've had to pull out because of work. So it's just me, my wife and our two boys now.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [noting it down] So that's four of you altogether, then.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: That's right.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [practical] And how old are the boys? We put life jackets on board, so I need to know which sizes to give you.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [thinking] Nine and twelve. Well, the younger one's nine now, but he'll be ten by August.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [noting it down] Two junior sizes, then. And they'll need to wear them on deck at all times, I'm afraid, even if they're strong swimmers.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [chuckles] They won't like that, but fair enough.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [practical] And when were you thinking of going? Our hire weeks run Saturday to Saturday.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [thinking aloud] Some time in August. We'd set off on Saturday the twenty-third, I think... [short pause] no, hang on, that's the day we'd have to be home. So we'd set off on the sixteenth.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [checking her screen] Departing the sixteenth of August, back on the twenty-third. Yes, I've got boats available that week. Now, which of our bases would suit you? There are three on this stretch of the canal.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [hopeful] The website mentioned Stoke Lock. That's the nearest one to us.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [apologetic] I'm afraid Stoke Lock is fully booked for the whole of August. And Abbey Basin isn't really an option either, because the canal's closed there until September while they replace the lock gates. [brighter] But we do have boats at Orchard Wharf, which is only about twenty minutes further on.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [agreeable] Orchard Wharf. That's fine, we're driving anyway.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [informative] Speaking of which, you can leave your car at the wharf while you're away. It's twelve pounds a day...

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [doing the sum aloud, slightly alarmed] Twelve a day? So that'd be, er, eighty-four for the week?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [reassuring] No, no. If you pay for the whole week up front, it's a flat rate of forty-five pounds. [slightly apologetic] It used to be free, but the landowner started charging last year.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [relieved] Forty-five. That's not bad at all. [hesitant] Er, one other thing that worries me. Do we need any experience? I've only ever rowed a dinghy on a boating lake.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [chuckles] You'd be surprised how many people say that. No experience needed. Before you leave, one of our staff spends about an hour on the boat with you, showing you how to steer and work the locks. Right, shall I tell you about the boats that are free that week?

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: Yes, please.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at Questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer Questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [reading from her screen] OK, there are three. The first is Kingfisher. She sleeps four, and she's the shortest of the three, which makes her much easier to handle. We often recommend her to beginners.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [interested] That sounds ideal, actually.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [candid] The one thing people do comment on is the space. The bedroom's fine, it's got a proper double bed, and the kitchen's very well equipped, but the shower is really tiny. [light laugh] If you're tall, you'll notice.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [wry] I'm six foot two, so... noted. And what does she cost?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [clearly] In June she'd be nine hundred and eighty pounds, but August is peak season, so for your week it's one thousand, one hundred and sixty.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [repeating, writing it down] One thousand one hundred and sixty. OK.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [moving on] The second is Moorhen, which sleeps six, so you'd all have more room to spread out. We used to provide a couple of kayaks with her, but there were rather too many, er, accidents, so these days she comes with two bicycles instead. They're handy for riding along the towpath to the village shops.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [enthusiastic] Oh, the boys would love that. Is there a catch?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [honest, measured] She's one of our older boats. I wouldn't say the engine's unreliable, because it was fully serviced in the spring, but it is quite loud, so whoever's steering at the back will hear it all day.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [chuckles] Fair enough. And the price for Moorhen?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: One thousand, three hundred and twenty-five for the week.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: Right.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [brightly] And the third is Heron, our newest boat. She was only launched in March, and she also sleeps six. People tend to assume she's got a washing machine, which she hasn't, but she does have a dishwasher, and that always goes down well.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [laughs] My wife would be thrilled. What's the downside?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [slightly apologetic] She's the longest boat in the fleet, so she can't turn round in some of the narrower sections, and you'd have to plan your route much more carefully. She's one thousand, four hundred and ninety.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [thinking aloud] Hmm. [short pause] I was leaning towards Kingfisher, but with my height... I think it'll be Moorhen. The bikes swing it, really.

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [pleased] Lovely, I'll reserve her for you now. We'll need a deposit of a quarter of the total within seven days, and I'll email you the paperwork this afternoon.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [warmly] Brilliant. Can I pay the deposit by card over the phone?

script.speaker: Lorna
script.text: [helpful] You can, or by bank transfer if you prefer. The details are on the confirmation email. The balance is then due six weeks before you travel.

script.speaker: Martin
script.text: [pleased] Card's easiest. Thanks so much for your help, Lorna.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Induction for Volunteer Theatre Ushers
parts.context: Monologue in an everyday social context (1 speaker)
parts.scenario: The front-of-house manager at a theatre gives an induction talk to a group of new volunteer ushers.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Diane
voices.desc: Front-of-house manager — female, 50s, energetic, organised, friendly but firm, occasionally wry; British accent (northern English, light)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear the front-of-house manager at a theatre giving an induction talk to some new volunteer ushers. First, you have some time to look at Questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [large echoey foyer, a few voices settling] [warm, projecting to a group] Right, good evening, everyone, and welcome to the Corran Theatre. I'm Diane, I run front of house, which means that for the next few months you'll be seeing rather a lot of me. [light laugh] Thank you all for volunteering.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [brisk, practical] We'll start with a quick tour of the ground floor, because the first thing audiences do is ask you where things are. So, we're standing just inside the main entrance, facing into the building. The box office is right here on your right, and the bar runs along the whole of the left-hand wall.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [explaining, a little wry] Now, the cloakroom. Regular visitors will tell you it's next to the box office, because that's where it used to be. It isn't any more; that space is now the shop, selling programmes and souvenirs. The cloakroom has moved to the opposite side, in the corner immediately to your left as you come through the doors, just before the bar begins.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [pointing the way verbally, clear] Straight ahead of us is the grand staircase, which takes you up to the circle, and on either side of it there's a set of double doors into the stalls. To the left of the staircase, a corridor runs all the way along the side of the auditorium, and there's a matching one on the right.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [friendly, informative] Let's take the left-hand corridor first. The first door you come to, on your left, says Technical Store. [firm] That's not ours, please don't go in there. Keep walking right to the far end, and the door facing you is the volunteers' room. That's where you'll leave your bags, sign in and get your briefing before each show.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [slightly amused] People are always surprised by where we've put the lift. You'd expect it beside the main staircase, wouldn't you? But it isn't. It's tucked away in the alcove at the far end of the bar, in the back left-hand corner of the foyer, so if someone in a wheelchair asks, send them past the bar, not towards the stairs.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [serious, measured] Now the right-hand corridor. About halfway along, on your right, is the first-aid room. [emphatic] Don't confuse it with the door at the very end of that corridor. That leads backstage to the stage door, and it's strictly for cast and crew.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [warmly] And finally, something we're rather proud of. The little room underneath the grand staircase, which you get into from the foyer, used to be a storage cupboard. We've turned it into a quiet room, for anyone, child or adult, who finds a performance overwhelming and needs a few minutes somewhere calm.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at Questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer Questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [practical, brisk] Right, a few things about the job itself. First, what you wear. We'll issue each of you with a burgundy waistcoat and a name badge. We used to hand out jackets, but under the stage lights they were far too hot. What you wear underneath is up to you, within reason: a plain white shirt, and dark trousers or a skirt.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [correcting a common assumption] Some of you may have heard that shirts must be black. That was the old rule, and it's gone. [firm but kind] Shoes, though: I know you're on your feet for three hours, but trainers aren't acceptable, I'm afraid. They need to be black and polished.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [thoughtful, slightly rueful] Latecomers. In the past, we'd simply take them in with a torch during the first scene, and it caused absolute chaos in the rows. So that's stopped. Now they wait until the stage manager radios through to say there's a suitable break, and until then they can follow the show on the monitor in the foyer.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [warning tone] And whatever you do, don't tell a latecomer they'll get their money back. Refunds aren't your decision; that's entirely up to the box office.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [conversational, then emphatic] The interval. People think the interval is all about ice creams, and yes, some of you will have a tray to sell from. But what I really need is for you to stay in your section and keep the aisles and exits clear, because that's when bags and coats start piling up and someone trips. [lighter] We did ask ushers to count the audience at one time, but that's done electronically from the tickets now.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [very serious, slowing down] Fire procedures. Our alarm has two stages. The first is an intermittent tone, and that's an alert only. You don't move anyone, and you don't say a word to the audience. You go straight to the exit you've been allocated on your rota and wait there.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [firm, clear] If the tone becomes continuous, that's when you evacuate your section. And you don't need to ring nine-nine-nine, because the system contacts the fire service automatically. Your job is people, not phone calls.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [encouraging, warmer] One last thing. I'd really encourage you all to come to the dress rehearsal on the twelfth. Now, it isn't so that you can see the show for nothing, although of course you will. And it's not really a chance to meet the actors either; they're far too busy and nervous to chat.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [earnest] The point is that you'll find out exactly when the sudden blackouts and the very loud effects happen. There's a gunshot in act two, for instance. If you know it's coming, you won't be caught out, and you can reassure anyone in your section who's startled.

script.speaker: Diane
script.text: [bright, wrapping up] Right, that's the talking done. Let's go and find those waistcoats, and then I'll walk you round so you can see it all for yourselves.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 2.

options.A: Volunteers must supply a dark-coloured shirt.

options.C: Volunteers may wear any footwear that is comfortable.

items.trap: A was the old rule (black shirts) and is now dropped; C is contradicted because trainers aren't acceptable.

options.B: explain how they can obtain a refund
options.C: direct them to a screen until they can be admitted

items.evidence: until then they can follow the show on the monitor in the foyer

options.A: making sure routes through the auditorium are unobstructed
options.C: keeping a record of audience numbers

items.evidence: keep the aisles and exits clear, because that's when bags and coats start piling up
items.trap: Some ushers do sell ice creams but it is not the main point; counting the audience was done in the past.

items.prompt: What should ushers do when they first hear the fire alarm?

options.A: start moving the audience out of the building
options.B: go to a specific exit and remain there

items.evidence: You go straight to the exit you've been allocated on your rota and wait there.
items.trap: A happens only at the second (continuous) stage; C is unnecessary because the system calls the fire service.

options.A: so that they can watch the production free of charge
options.B: so that they can be introduced to the cast

items.evidence: you'll find out exactly when the sudden blackouts and the very loud effects happen

parts.title: River Erosion Field-Trip Report
parts.scenario: Two geography students, Hannah and Callum, discuss the draft of their field-trip report on river bank erosion with their lecturer, Dr Mercer.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Dr Mercer
voices.desc: Geography lecturer — female, 50s, direct, dry humour, supportive but exacting; British RP accent

voices.label: Hannah
voices.desc: Student — female, early 20s, keen, quick, a little anxious; British accent (southern English)

voices.label: Callum
voices.desc: Student — male, early 20s, laid-back, frank, sceptical; clearly Scottish accent (en-GB)

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two geography students, Hannah and Callum, talking to their lecturer, Dr Mercer, about their field-trip report on river erosion. First, you have some time to look at Questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [small office, a door closing softly] [friendly, brisk] Come in, both of you, sit down. So, I've read your draft on the erosion fieldwork at Ashcombe. There's a lot of good material in it, but structurally it needs some work, so let's go through it section by section.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [keen, slightly nervous] Great, thanks. We were a bit worried about the length, actually.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [dry] Rightly so. Let's start with the site description.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [frank, relaxed] I did wonder if we could just cut that altogether. Everyone on the module knows the site. We all went there on the same day.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [patient, a touch dry] Your external examiner didn't, though. No, it needs to stay. But at the moment it's sitting on its own and repeating half of what's already in your introduction. I'd fold the two together into a single section.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [agreeing] That makes sense. One tidy section rather than two half-empty ones.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [conceding, good-humoured] Fair enough.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [moving on] Then the methods. Now, this is very thorough...

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [anxious, cutting in] Too thorough? Should we shorten it?

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [reassuring] I wouldn't cut a word of it, actually. It's accurate, and someone could repeat your study from it. The trouble is that three pages on calibrating a flow meter interrupt the reader just when they want your argument. Keep a short summary in the main text, and put the step-by-step detail at the back, after the references.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [making a note] Right, so the full procedure gets tucked in at the end as supplementary material.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [more serious] Next, your velocity and discharge results. [short pause] This is where I have real concerns. Your discharge figures are roughly a hundred times too big.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [slightly defensive] Aye, we wondered about that. Hannah thought the flow meter might've been faulty. Could we get one of the technicians to look at it?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [quickly] I did think that at first, but...

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [firm but kind] There's nothing wrong with the meter. I've checked the log, and it was calibrated the day before you went out. The problem is that you measured the channel width in centimetres and the depth in metres and then multiplied them. So it's the working-out that has to be done again, from scratch.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [groans] Oh no. That's embarrassing.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [lightly] It happens every year. Sediment analysis, now. The sieving results look plausible, but the weights for samples four, five and six are oddly identical, which makes me wonder whether the balance was misbehaving that day.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [thinking aloud] Could we add some close-up photos of the samples? Then people could see the difference in grain size for themselves.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [doubtful] Pictures won't tell anyone what anything weighs. Before you change a single number, take your raw data to Julia, the technician in the soils lab. She looks after the balances, and she'll tell you whether those readings can be trusted.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [agreeing] I'll email her today.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [practical] And should we wait to hear from her before we touch the discussion? Because if those weights change, our whole argument about grain size changes too.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [approving] Exactly. Don't rewrite anything that depends on those samples until she's had a look.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [hesitant] And the evaluation? We're well over the word limit, so I was thinking we could just drop it.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [firm] Absolutely not. It's a required section, and you'd lose marks. But it's currently longer than your results, which is the wrong way round. Bring it down to about half its present length, and focus on the two or three limitations that really matter.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [wry chuckle] So halve it, don't bin it.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at Questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer Questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [curious] Remind me why you chose that stretch of river. It's not the most obvious site.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [thoughtful] Partly access. There's a footpath right down to the bank, so carrying all the kit was easy. But honestly, if that'd been the only thing, we'd have gone to the bridge site, which is even easier to get to.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [enthusiastic] What actually decided it was that the department has records from exactly that stretch going back to the nineteen-nineties, so we could set our results against theirs. The meanders are lovely and pronounced as well, but that wasn't really why.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [measured] Good. Now, your erosion pins. You put twelve into the outer bank in March and measured them again in September.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [defensive] We know twelve isn't many.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [reassuring, then serious] Actually, I don't think the number's the issue; twelve is perfectly respectable for a project this size. And you mention cattle possibly knocking them, but you said yourselves the field was fenced off. What worries me is that March to September misses the winter floods, and that's when most bank erosion takes place.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [quietly] Right. We hadn't thought of that.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [kindly] Don't panic. You can't go back and measure in January now, but you must acknowledge it, and say what you'd expect a winter record to show.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [turning to him] Callum, how did you feel when you saw the outer bank figures?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [candid] Honestly? I'd expected the bank to have retreated by tens of centimetres, from everything in the textbooks, and it had hardly moved at all. [short pause] It's not that I doubted the readings. We measured every pin twice. And they're nothing like the department's older figures either, which showed much faster retreat.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [probing] So how are you going to explain that difference from the earlier data?

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [confident] I think it's the stone wall the landowner built upstream about ten years ago. It's protecting the bank, so there's less energy reaching our site.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [politely disagreeing] I'm not convinced. The wall's three hundred metres upstream. I'd say it's simply been a run of drier years, so there's been lower discharge.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [sighs, half-laughing] We've been going round in circles on that for a week.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [amused] Well, at least you agree on everything else. You're both happy with scatter graphs for the results?

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: Aye, no argument there.

script.speaker: Hannah
script.text: [warmly] And we both want to keep the bits from our conversation with the farmer. That was really useful.

script.speaker: Dr Mercer
script.text: [thoughtful] Then present both explanations and weigh them up. And before you submit... I'd normally suggest swapping drafts with another group, but nobody else worked on your stretch, so that won't help much. Your reference list is fine; don't touch it. What I'd like you to do is read Pearson's article on artificial bank protection. It'll give you the evidence to judge Hannah's theory properly.

script.speaker: Callum
script.text: [good-humoured, Scottish lilt] Great. More reading. [chuckles] No, fair enough. Thanks, Dr Mercer.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: The Economics of the Medieval English Wool Trade
parts.scenario: A lecturer in economic history gives a talk on the economics of the English wool trade in the Middle Ages.

voices.label: Narrator
voices.desc: Test narrator — neutral, clear, measured British RP; the same voice in every test

voices.label: Lecturer
voices.desc: Economic history lecturer — male, 50s, articulate, measured, engaging with dry wit; British RP accent

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer giving a talk about the economics of the medieval English wool trade. First, you have some time to look at Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer Questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lecture theatre, a faint murmur fading] [clear, engaging] Good morning. Today we're turning to what was, for several centuries, the backbone of the English economy: wool. One historian remarked that England in this period was little more than a sheep farm with a government attached. [wry] An exaggeration, certainly, but not a huge one.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining, steady] So why was English wool so sought after? It wasn't a question of volume; later on, Spain produced considerably more. Nor was it the colour, which actually varied a good deal from region to region. What buyers in Flanders and Italy were paying for was its fineness, by which I mean how thin and soft the individual fibres were, because that determined the quality of the cloth they could weave.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [measured] Now, you might assume that the great flocks belonged to the aristocracy, to earls and barons with vast estates. Some did, of course. But the really large-scale producers were monasteries, particularly those of the Cistercian order, some of which kept ten or fifteen thousand sheep on the uplands of Yorkshire and the Welsh borders.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative, giving figures] Wool was traded by the sack, a standard unit of about three hundred and sixty-four pounds in weight, or roughly the fleeces of two hundred and fifty sheep. At its peak, in the early fourteenth century, England was exporting somewhere in the region of thirty-five thousand sacks a year.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [interested, building] What's economically fascinating is how these monasteries sold their wool. Italian and Flemish merchants would pay for it in advance, sometimes for the next ten or even twenty years' production. [short pause] Now, this wasn't strictly a loan, and it wasn't really investment in the modern sense either. Economic historians generally describe it as a form of credit: the abbeys were, in effect, borrowing against wool that hadn't yet grown.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [cautionary] And this was a risky arrangement. If an epidemic swept through a flock, an abbey could find itself owing years of wool that it simply couldn't deliver. The term contemporaries used for these outbreaks was murrain. That's M... U... double R... A... I... N. It was a rather vague word, covering almost any disease of cattle or sheep, and several abbeys were left heavily in debt by murrain in the late thirteenth century.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [signposting, shifting topic] Let's turn now to the Crown, because English kings were very quick to see wool as a source of revenue. Export duties on wool became one of the largest items of royal income. [sceptical] It's often said that this money went into building castles, but in fact remarkably little did. Overwhelmingly, it paid for military campaigns, above all Edward the Third's campaigns in France during the Hundred Years' War.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [informative] To manage all this, the Crown created what was called the Staple: a single designated town through which all wool exports had to pass. The Staple moved around a great deal at first, between Bruges, Antwerp and a number of English ports, but from thirteen sixty-three it was fixed at Calais, then an English possession, and it remained there for almost two hundred years.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [analytical, emphasising the contrast] Officially, the Staple existed to guarantee quality, so that foreign buyers could trust what they were getting. That was the justification. [slight emphasis] But the real motive was far more practical. With all the wool passing through one place, collection of the tax became much simpler, and far harder to evade.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [dry, amused] The merchants who ran the Staple became extremely wealthy, and they regularly lent money to the king, sometimes in return for reductions in the very duties they were supposed to be paying. So the relationship between the Crown and the wool merchants was, shall we say, rather cosy.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [transitional] Now, these heavy duties on raw wool had an important side effect. Finished cloth was taxed much more lightly, so it increasingly made sense to weave the cloth in England and export that instead. And this shift was helped along by a change in a process called fulling. Fulling means beating woven cloth in water to thicken and clean it, and traditionally it was done by workers trampling it with their feet.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [explaining] By the fourteenth century, fulling was increasingly mechanised. Wind power was tried in some flatter areas, but it proved too unreliable. The mills that succeeded were driven by water, which is why the cloth industry gradually drifted away from the old towns towards hilly districts with fast-flowing streams, such as the Cotswolds and the Pennine valleys.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [warmer, anecdotal] You can still see the profits of all this today. Wealthy wool and cloth merchants spent lavishly on their parish churches, and the so-called wool churches of Suffolk and the Cotswolds are strikingly large for such small villages. If you visit, notice that it isn't spires that dominate; spires are actually quite rare in these areas. What you see are tall, elaborately decorated towers, often paid for by a single merchant family.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [thoughtful] One more factor deserves a mention. After the Black Death in thirteen forty-eight, labour became scarce and expensive, and many landowners turned their fields over from crops to sheep, since a single shepherd could look after land that had once needed dozens of farm workers. That kept wool production high, even as exports of raw wool began to fall.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [reflective] Finally, decline. By the sixteenth century, English raw wool no longer dominated European markets. Partly that was because English weavers were now using so much of it themselves. But there was also serious competition from Spain, where a breed with an exceptionally fine fleece had been developed. Spanish merino wool gradually took over the luxury end of the market.

script.speaker: Lecturer
script.text: [lighter, wrapping up] The legacy of the trade survives in some odd places. The Lord Speaker in the House of Lords still sits on the Woolsack, a large cushion stuffed with wool, as a reminder of where England's wealth once came from. [brisk] Next week, we'll look at how the cloth industry developed in its own right.

script.speaker: Narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test. You now have two minutes to check your answers.
